en: Regarding the introductory narrative and meaning of the *Caturvargika-prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
according to an examination of the *Caturvargika-vinaya-piṭaka*, when the World-Honored One first preached the *Prātimokṣa*,
Śāriputra inquired about the past seven Buddhas, asking which of their teachings would endure long in the world and which would not.
The World-Honored One replied that by establishing the precepts and reciting them, the Dharma would endure for a long time in the world;
had they not been established and recited, the Buddha-dharma would have quickly perished. This is how the precepts originated.

Generally, the Vinaya does not set forth rules in advance, but rather establishes them only after a bhikṣu has committed an offense; thus, offenses are determined according to actual facts. Consequently, individuals...
Because his heart was won over, Śāriputra earnestly requested that [the Buddha] speak; the Buddha replied that it was not the right time.
It is also said that the Buddha knows the time himself, implying that he establishes the rules only after waiting for the appropriate moment.
Generally, while various sūtras may be spoken by Bodhisattvas to one another, the Vinaya alone is spoken by the Buddha himself.

Why is it that he does not dare to add a single word? It is like the worldly principle that when rites, music, military expeditions, and punishments proceed from the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords fold their hands and obey, and the world is well-governed;

but when these proceed from the feudal lords or high ministers, the four barbarian tribes invade one after another, and the people have no place to set their hands or feet. The Vinaya taught by the Buddha is likewise.
The precepts established by the Buddha are for ten reasons: first, to bring the Saṃgha together; second, to cause the Saṃgha to rejoice;

third, to cause the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness; fourth, to inspire faith in those who have not yet believed; fifth, to increase the faith of those who already believe; sixth, to discipline those who are difficult to tame;

seventh, to bring peace and happiness to those who possess a sense of shame and remorse; eighth, to sever present outflows (āsrava); ninth, to sever future outflows; [tenth, to realize the unsurpassed noble path].
The ten impure things that come forth cause the True Dharma to abide long in the world; therefore, at the conclusion of each precept, this point is first clarified.
The holy assembly on Vulture Peak is a sandalwood forest—how could there be ill-formed, common wood? This is surely because [the Buddha] foresaw the future.
I am but a piece of worldy wood, crooked and knotted; therefore, the Great Compassionate One first showed me the guiding line and nurtured me through skillful means.
Let those of later generations take this as a model for their own minds and do not harbor doubts regarding the Sage’s era.
The Meaning of the Origins of the *Caturvargika-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, compiled by Guangmo, disciple of Yunqi. Regarding the four parts:
first, the Bhikṣu Precepts; second, the Bhikṣuṇī Precepts; third, the *Varṣā-khandaka* (Chapter on the Rainy Season Retreat); and fourth, the *Śayanāsana-vastu* (Chapter on Lodgings).
The *Śayanāsana-vastu* (here translated as *Shajian-du*) means "Collection of Dharmas" (*Dharmaskandha*), referring to the gathering of various categories of dharmas together in one place.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is the fundamental basis for the individual practice of the bhikṣu precepts. Regarding its origin from the Dharmaguptaka school:
it was first established thirty-eight years after the Buddha’s enlightenment when he attended a royal feast in Rājagṛha.
When the meal was finished, the Buddha had Rāhula wash his bowl; he dropped it by accident, and it shattered into five pieces on the ground.
The Buddha prophesied: "After my parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣus shall divide my Vinaya into five schools.
One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Upagupta had five disciples who indeed divided the Buddha’s Vinaya into [five parts].
The five schools are: first, the Dharmaguptaka; second, the Sarvāstivāda; third, the Kāśyapīya; fourth, the Mahīśāsaka;
and fifth, the Vātsīputrīya. The present edition belongs to the Dharmaguptaka school. "Dharmaguptaka" is translated here as "Dharma-secrecy.
The initial verse of the current text was edited and finalized by Vinaya Master Xuánzàng and is not the original version from the canon.
Verse: The First Precept on Celibacy. It originated with the Venerable Sūdena. After his father had passed away, his mother urged him to abandon the precepts and return home.
The Venerable One was unwilling; though his mother urged him repeatedly, the Venerable One ultimately refused. His mother said: "As for..."
Unwilling to turn back, he agreed to serve as the seed. At that time, before the Buddha had yet established the precepts, the Venerable One consented to his mother’s command.
His wife approached the Venerable One three times and performed the act; consequently, she obtained a son, who was named Bījaka after the seed.

Later, he too went forth and attained the Way, becoming known as the Venerable Bījaka. It was because of this that the Buddha subsequently established the precepts for those who share the same precepts and common precepts.
The Tibetan edition lacks the character "戒" (śīla) in the phrase "共下," reading instead simply "共比丘同戒" (samāna-śīla with bhikṣus).
This means "sharing the same precepts" (*samāna-śīla*) with other bhikṣus—referring to the shared precepts, the common precepts, and the individual shared precepts.

Regarding "not abandoning the precepts" (*a-pratyākhyāta-śīla*), the Buddha stated that if a bhikṣu does not delight in pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), he is permitted to abandon the precepts and return to lay life; however, if he does not abandon the precepts, nor [if his] precepts are merely weak (*durbala*) and he does not [himself]...
To repent for having committed an impure act constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bhikṣu, such that he may not dwell together with others;
this includes cases involving animals. Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu practicing meditative concentration in the forest when a female macaque became familiar and playful before him.

As the bhikṣu went on his rounds, he observed her and reported it to the Buddha, who established a rule accordingly; thus, these words were spoken: "Pārājika," which is translated here as "abandonment" (*qi*).
Because a person whose head has been severed cannot be restored to life, they are called "abandoned" (*pārājika*).

"Not living together" means not performing the same *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) nor reciting the same *prātimokṣa* (code of discipline) with other bhikṣus; one does not dwell together with them in these two matters. The following cases are to be understood by analogy.
2. The Precept Against Stealing: It originated when the Venerable Dhanika, for the sake of building a private meditation cell for himself, took timber belonging to the king without permission.
When the matter was later discovered, this bhikṣu was apprehended under the laws of the state; according to the law, stealing five coins constituted a capital offense.
However, because he was a bhikṣu, the king merely reprimanded him and sent him away, hence the mention of his being "driven out of the country."

The Third Precept on Killing: It originated within the Veṇuvana (Bamboo Grove) Monastery when various bhikṣus, having heard the Buddha teach the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), contemplated and practiced it accordingly.
They developed a profound loathing for their physical bodies; though they sought death, they could not find it.
As they searched for a blade to commit suicide, there was the bhikṣu Muḷakadevīya, who was of a non-Buddhist lineage. Carrying a knife, he entered the grove, and a bhikṣu requested his assistance.

Having taken his own life, he used his robes and bowl to repay [the debt]; because he thus took the lives of more than sixty monks, a lay devotee happened to be wandering about and saw corpses filling the garden.
Suspecting they were bhikṣus who had been collectively killed, he gave rise to criticism and disdain.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, therefore established the precept.
The Fourth Precept on False Speech: It originated during a time of famine when food was difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain through almsround.
The Buddha commanded them to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in various locations. At that time, the bhikṣus in the Pārileyyaka Garden secretly deliberated on a stratagem to easily obtain food;
they went to the houses of lay devotees and claimed, "I have attained the state of a superior person" (and so forth), while remaining in the latter rains retreat.

Eventually, having approached the World-Honored One, he was questioned regarding this matter; consequently, [the Buddha] established the rule excluding those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and one bhikṣu who, out of shame for not yet having attained the Path, falsely claimed to have attained it later.

Through diligent effort, he truly realized the fruit of Arhatship and doubted whether his previous false statement had been overweening pride. Now, although he has truly realized it, he remains uncertain as to whether he committed an offense or not.
He addressed the Buddha to resolve his doubts, and the Buddha explained for him, saying: "There is no offense in this case; apart from this, all others constitute an offense.
Thus ends the section on the four *pārājika* (grave) precepts.
**Thirteen *Saṃghāvaśeṣa*:** *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* is translated as "remaining with the community" (*zhòngcán*); it refers to those matters that must be settled by the *saṃgha*.
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* is translated as "residual" (*avaśeṣa*). It is like a vessel that is damaged and no longer fit for use;
the Saṃgha is the vessel for the Path, and if it is damaged, its golden virtue is incomplete.
First: This [offense] originated with the Venerable Kālodāyin, who, out of lustful intent, played and emitted semen. The Buddha knew this.
For this reason, another bhikṣu, suspecting that he had violated this precept because he had emitted semen in a dream, reported his doubt to the Buddha for resolution;
it was to exclude such cases as non-offenses that the words "except in a dream" were included.
Second: Furthermore, when a man was led by women into a room to view it while they waited outside the door, he then made physical contact and stroked their bodies;
because the Buddha knew of this, he established the precept.
Third, it was also established because of the previous person’s act of leading a woman into a room and using coarse, vulgar speech.
Fourth, it was also established because of that same previous person.
Fifth, it was established because of what occurred involving the Venerable Kāla.
Sixth: While the Buddha was on Vulture Peak Mountain, he permitted the bhikṣus to each build their own dwellings.
There was one bhikṣu who, while building his dwelling, personally hewed down a tree. The tree deity had many sons and grandsons; the deity thought to himself, "This bhikṣu is cutting down my tree;
my descendants will have no place to rely. He then intended to strike the bhikṣu, but then reflected again: "If I strike this bhikṣu, I shall incur sin."
He went to inform the World-Honored One and related his intention in detail. The Buddha praised him, saying, "Excellent! The Buddha said, "Go now quickly to the banks of the Ganges.
There is a great tree named Śāla; that deity has just passed away, and you may take up residence there.
It was on this account that the Buddha established the precept.
Seventh: It originated with the Venerable Channa and King Udayana, the friend of kings, who wished to construct a large dwelling.
Because Channa relied upon property belonging to others, there was a great tree in the city of Kauśāmbī where carriages, horses, and travelers constantly rested.
Channa cut it down, which everyone criticized and found offensive; the Buddha, knowing this, established the precept.

Eighth: When the Buddha was at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, the Venerable Trapusa Māra-putra, knowing the sequence of the bedding, furniture, and rooms for the assembly, assigned them to the monks for their meals.
A bhikṣu named Maitrī arrived late and received a poor room, poor bedding, and poor food.
Suspecting that the Venerable had a heart of favoritism and aversion, he used his sister, the bhikṣuṇī Maitrī, as a pretext.
"Pārājika slander" refers to baseless claims, meaning they lack any foundation; this is because among the three criteria of seeing, hearing, or suspecting, none are present.
Since that venerable one was an Arhat endowed with pure conduct, and he intended to destroy that purity out of a mind of hatred, the Buddha heard of it and established this rule.

Ninth: This refers again to the previous matter concerning the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra. After his disciplinary proceedings were concluded, he descended from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and saw a ram mating with a ewe.
He compared the ram to Vatsa and the ewe to Maitrāyaṇī, and subsequently slandered her again, claiming, "I saw it with my own eyes.
Since sheep are fundamentally of a different species, this is called a "case of a different category" (*anyabhāga*).
"To take a portion from among the various [categories]" means that one takes a small part of something similar from among the different [categories];

since it is not an actual offense, it is called "not a *pārājika* slander. Generally, those who share the same surname, the same name, or the same appearance are all termed "differentiated parts" (*bhinnabhāga*).
Tenth: Regarding the first phrase, "originating from Devadatta," this refers to the thought of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha.
As for the question of by what means this could be accomplished, the second phrase states: "The methods for breaking the Saṃgha consist of five practices:

(1) begging for alms for as long as one lives; (2) wearing rag-robes for as long as one lives; (3) sitting in the open air for as long as one lives; (4) not consuming butter for as long as one lives..."
The five practices—refraining from salt, abstaining from fish and meat for as long as one lives, and so forth—appear on the surface to be virtuous dharmas;
however, because they establish a mind that rejects these [true teachings] to follow those [false ones], they are called "dharmas that destroy the Sangha.

By means of such hypocrisy, they deceive the ranks of beginners who cannot distinguish truth from falsehood, leading them to believe these practices are real and to follow them. This is like Wang Mang’s feigned humility and deference.
The Śrāmaṇera asked: "Is this in accordance with the Dharma or contrary to it?
The Buddha established [this rule] for this reason. Eleventh: "The remaining associates" refers to the remaining associates of the aforementioned person.
There were four remaining associates of Devadatta: first, Maṇḍikada; second, Khaṇḍadravya; third, Kokālika; and fourth, Kaṭamorakatiṣya.

Raurukeśa. Twelfth: [The two elders] named Aśvajit and Pūrṇaśas, who resided in the village of Kāliṅga, practiced evil deeds themselves—such as planting flowers and trees—and taught others to plant flowers and trees.
Irrigating [the garden] for others and irrigating for oneself; picking flowers and stringing them for others and picking flowers and stringing them for oneself;
holding a flower garland and giving it to others and holding a flower garland and giving it to others;

sitting together with a woman, desiring food, laughing, engaging in miscellaneous chatter, and performing various kinds of unwholesome conduct—all these are termed "corrupting families" (*kuladūṣaka*). "Corrupting families" refers to those who defile households.
There are four kinds [of corrupting families]: first, corrupting a family based on the household itself, which means obtaining goods from that family and giving them to this family;
giving to one family and not giving to another; the one to whom they are given rejoices, while the one to whom they are not given becomes angry.

Second, corrupting a family based on material gain, which means that whatever gains a bhikṣu obtains, he gives to one family and does not give to another; the one to whom they are given rejoices, while the one to whom they are not given... [becomes angry].
Third, based on relatives, one defiles a household; that is, a bhikṣu is friendly with a king’s minister and protects one family while not protecting another.
Those whom he protects rejoice, while those he does not protect become angry. Fourth, based on the monastery, one defiles a household;

that is, a bhikṣu takes property from the monastery and gives it to one family while not giving it to another. Those to whom he gives it rejoice, while those to whom he does not give it become angry. If...
There is no offense for one who plants flowers as an offering to the Triple Gem.
Thirteenth: This originated with the Venerable Channa.
In the text of the formal resolution (*karmavācanā*), *pārivāsika* is translated here as "separate dwelling" (*bie zhu*); this means that the various bhikṣus do not rise together with him.

*Śamatha-mānatva* (止也摩那埵) is translated as "mental joy" (*yi-xi*). This refers to the fact that when a bhikṣu commits an offense and undergoes the corresponding punishment, joy arises in the minds of the assembly.
Thus concludes the thirteen [offenses] involving the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community).
II. The Two Indeterminate Dharmas (*aniyata-dharma*). "Indeterminate" means that among the three categories of offenses, the disciplinary treatment is not fixed.
The first: When the Buddha was at Jetavana, Kālodāyin had a close female friend from his lay life named Ciñcā-māṇavikā;
they were intimate with one another. Even after the Venerable One had gone forth [into homelessness], he continued to frequent her.
When the day came, they sat together in a secluded place and spoke improper words.

A neighboring laywoman of right faith named Viśākhā heard these improper words and also caught sight of them sitting together (as detailed below). The three rules are those set forth immediately below.
The second [category] is also for those who sit exposed to the elements as mentioned before; thus, they are exempted from the *pārājika* offense and are instead governed by two rules.
Thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses: *Niḥsargika-pāyattika* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "forfeiture and expiation.
These thirty matters all concern the punishment of offenses regarding clothing and requisites; the robes and requisites of the monk who has committed the offense must be forfeited.

To relinquish an offense within the Saṃgha constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture and confession). One who forfeits such a robe is subject to punishment and discipline;

yet, by relinquishing it, one is exempted from the full gravity of the downfall, which is why it is termed *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Regarding the legal rules for the forfeiture of robes, it states: "This robe subject to forfeiture must be surrendered to the Saṃgha.
It must be surrendered within the assembly; it should not be surrendered to a single individual. One must go before the Saṃgha to perform the surrender."
Baring the right shoulder and removing one’s sandals, one should pay homage to the senior monk by kneeling on the ground with palms joined and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* regarding a certain matter.

I now relinquish this robe or bowl to the Saṃgha. Having finished relinquishing the robe, one should perform the confession (*pratideśanā*). The person receiving the confession should then make the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Afterwards, when receiving the confession, one should announce: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu so-and-so has committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* regarding such-and-such a matter.
He now offers this robe or bowl to the Saṃgha. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me permission to receive the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
Having made this announcement, one should then receive the confession and speak to that person as follows:
Self-reproaching his own mind, he replied, "I have respectfully heard your instruction.
First: When the Buddha was at Jetavana, he did not permit bhikṣus to keep extra robes (*atirekacīvara*). At that time, the group of six bhikṣus (*ṣaḍvargika*) intentionally kept extra robes;
they changed their garments during the morning, midday, and afternoon sessions before entering the assembly. A bhikṣu who practices contentment raised a formal announcement (*jñapti*) against them.
The World-Honored One therefore established the first phrase, "the robes are already finished," which refers to the three robes of a bhikṣu being complete.
*Kāṭhina* is translated as "merit" (*guṇa*); all those who perform pure donations (*śuddha-dakṣiṇā*) are called "merit," meaning that the extra robe has been properly dedicated.

"Withdrawal" (*niḥsaraṇa*) refers to the act of relinquishing it; thus, this refers to the communal recitation of the sūtra concerning the acquisition of extra robes, which permits their storage for ten days.
When the Buddha established this precept, Ānanda obtained a highly valued *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) which he wished to offer to Mahākāśyapa;
however, as Kāśyapa was practicing *dhūta* austerities elsewhere and was not present, Ānanda hesitated, fearing that by keeping the robe without offering it, he might violate the precept.
He went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha asked Kāśyapa when he would return, and he replied, "In ten days."
The Buddha further permitted that one may keep [the robes] for ten days; however, if one does not give them away after ten days, it constitutes an offense.
Second: This originated when the group of six bhikṣus left their three robes with a bhikṣu who was a relative and went wandering among the people.
The bhikṣu who had received the robes feared that insects would damage or ruin them through moisture, so he dried them in the sun during the day. The other [bhikṣus] [complained].

The Venerable Kāśyapa asked him, "The Buddha has established a rule forbidding the keeping of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*); how can this be? The person who had received the deposit replied (as follows).
He then informed the Buddha, who had previously established this precept. At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu who had business to attend to and wished to go among the people;
however, his three robes were heavy and he could not carry them while traveling. He informed the Buddha, and because of this, the Buddha convened [the assembly].

Because the assembly performs the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) to establish the rule for not losing one's robe, it says: "Except by a formal act of the Saṃgha.
Here, *karman* means "formal procedure" (the two types of *karman* are: first, the adjudication of offenses; second, the conferral of joy; subsequent instances follow this pattern).

Third: It originated because a certain bhikṣu had worn out his great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and was making a new one; since he could not complete it within ten days, he was unable to discard the old one immediately.
Because he informed the Buddha of this matter, the rule was established permitting him to keep it for up to one month to reach completion.
Regarding "out-of-season robes" (*akālacīvara*): these are robes that were not received during the proper time for giving robes; if one desires them, they may be accepted at any time.
"Having received it, one quickly completes it" means that if one desires an out-of-season robe, one receives it and immediately sets about making it.
If it cannot be completed within ten days, another month is permitted so that it may be fully finished.
Fourth: When she saw a bhikṣu whose patched robe was torn and tattered, the bhikṣuṇī Padmavarṇā felt a heart of compassion.
She took off her own fine-colored upper garment and exchanged it for his tattered robe, putting it on herself.
Upon approaching the Buddha, the Buddha asked, "Why are you wearing this tattered robe? The bhikṣuṇī recounted the preceding circumstances, and the Buddha said to her:
When robes were sufficient and there was a surplus, it was permitted to give them away. Why? Because when a woman wears fine upper garments, she still feels aversion toward them;

how much more so for tattered ones? Therefore, the Buddha established this rule. Once the Buddha had established it, the bhikṣus, out of caution and fear, did not dare to take robes from nuns who were their relatives.
The Buddha then further established the three-character restriction: "not a relative. At that time, within the Jeta Grove...
When monks and nuns of the two assemblies received donated robes and were dividing them, it occurred that the men received women’s robes and the women received men’s robes.
When the nuns offered these robes to the monks in exchange, the monks did not dare to trade with them.
The Buddha then permitted such exchanges.
Fifth: It originated with Kāḷudāyin, who, having looked at the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā with lustful intent, caused her to become stained.
When she washed his clothes, her conduct was indecent, and the other bhikṣuṇīs complained about it. They informed the Buddha, and he established a rule for all bhikṣus.
Consequently, [the bhikṣus] did not dare to have their relatives, the bhikṣuṇīs, wash or dye their clothes; the Buddha further prohibited this.
The sixth [type of] words from kinsmen:
It originated when a certain elder in Śrāvastī, who was a close friend of the Venerable Bhadanta-Bāṣpa-Nanda, went to the Jeta Grove to visit him;
the Venerable One preached the sublime Dharma for him, and because he attained the joy of the Dharma, [he spoke these words].
When he wished to offer something to the Venerable One, the latter declined it. He then earnestly entreated him, saying, "What do you require?

[The Venerable One] replied, "I shall accept only the garment you are wearing. That garment was of great value. He said, "Wait until I have returned home, and I will immediately send it to be offered.
Why was this? Because he entered the city without external ornaments. The Venerable One then desired it; he, having no other choice, took it off.
As he was departing separately to enter the city, a gatekeeper asked, "Has the householder been robbed? Why do you return wearing such tattered clothes?
The householder falsely replied, "I was robbed by bandits outside the gate of Jeta’s Grove. The gatekeeper immediately intended to pursue them, but the householder recounted the matter to him.
Those who heard this criticized and disparaged him; when the Buddha heard of it, he established a precept so that the bhikṣus would not dare [to act in such a manner].
When [the Buddha] was asked for robes by a householder, he further established a rule by adding the phrase "unless it is from one who is not a relative," thereby excluding other circumstances.

He established that there are times [when this is permitted]: when various bhikṣus, having completed their summer retreat, came to visit the Buddha; during the heat of the day they traveled at night and were robbed of their robes.

The Buddha further opened the allowance for circumstances such as being robbed, lost, burned, or swept away by water. This constitutes the case of requesting robes from a householder without committing an offense.
Seventh: A certain bhikṣu whose robes had been stolen went naked to the gate of Jetavana, accompanied by many other bhikṣus who had also been robbed of their robes.
When the lay devotees heard of this, they brought many fine robes to offer as alms. Another bhikṣu then took them by stealth and gave them to the group of six bhikṣus (Ṣaḍvargika).
The Buddha, having heard of this, established the rule that one may accept many robes from those who have made a formal invitation to do so.
This refers to lay devotees who, having first invited the monks at their own discretion to receive many robes, do not limit themselves to taking only one or two;
therefore, it is said below that "one should receive with contentment.
Eighth: [The case] involving Upananda, concerning whom a lay devotee heard that he was being provided with the price for a robe.

The following day, he went straight to that house (and so forth). That lay devotee then conceived a feeling of resentment and said, "I was privately discussing future matters when I invited you at your leisure;
why did the bhikṣu arrive first and speak [of them]? The Buddha heard of this and therefore established the rule.

Ninth: It was also because of the person [who had previously] heard that the two householders were preparing the price for robes (and so forth), and because the Buddha heard of it, he established the rule.
Tenth: It was also because of the person [who had previously] heard that there was a high minister in the city of Rājagṛha who was a close friend of the Venerable One.
A messenger was sent to deliver the price for robes to the Venerable One. The Venerable One immediately dispatched this same messenger to have a certain elder receive the funds on his behalf.
Later, the chief minister questioned the messenger, asking, "Has the robe-price you were sent with been used to purchase robes?
The messenger replied as he had before. The minister then sent the messenger back again, saying, "If no robes have been purchased, you may take the original price and return."
Upon hearing this, the Venerable went to the householder’s place to collect the payment for the robe. Just as he was about to take it, the householder had some business and went out;

hearing that the robe price was being collected, he said, "Wait a moment until I return. When the Venerable asked why there was such an agreement, the householder replied, "If you go late, you must pay five hundred gold coins.
The Venerable agreed to this condition. The householder, having no other choice, took the robe and gave it to him. Then...
Because they departed too late, they were consequently fined five hundred coins; the assembly all censured them and informed the Buddha, who therefore established this rule.
Eleventh: When the Buddha was in the country of Kalandaka, the group of six bhikṣus made new bedding from wild silkworm cotton.
They went to a silkworm-raising household to purchase it, saying to the householders, "The silkworms are not yet mature; wait a little longer. Those bhikṣus waited there, spying on them.
Beside them, a silkworm-keeper, being in a hurry, exposed the cocoons and chrysalises to the sun; they became distressed with heat and made a noise.
When the lay follower Zhengxin saw this, he disapproved of it, and the Buddha heard of it and therefore established a precept.
Twelfth: In the city of Vaiśālī, many young men were prone to sexual misconduct and excessive desire;
they made blankets from pure black sheep’s wool to wrap around their bodies so that people could not see them while traveling at night.
The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks imitated them, also making bedding from pure black sheep’s wool. When the young men saw this, they disparaged it, saying, "We are superior."
"Monks, do you also take pleasure in sexual misconduct, that for this reason you have committed such acts? Hearing this, the Buddha prohibited it.
(The term *nau* is pronounced like the sound of a ram. Thirteen: The six groups of monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) again made new bedding out of pure white wool.

The laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying, "These bhikṣus are addicted to wealth and pleasure like kings or high ministers. The Buddha heard of this and therefore established the prohibition.
In the *Pāṅ* (or *Māṅ*) commentary on the Vinaya, it is also written as *māng*; it means a dog of brindled color with much fur, for the term is taken from its coat color.

The fourteenth [case]: When the Buddha was at Jetavana, the six groups of monks (ṣaḍvargika) were dissatisfied with their bedding—whether it was too heavy or too light, too thin or too thick—and desired to make new bedding. A monk who practiced contentment (saṃtuṣṭa-bhikṣu) disapproved of this and informed the Buddha;
therefore, the rule was established, excepting the case of a formal monastic act (saṃghakarma). Specifically, for a sick monk, his old bedding may be considered discarded refuse (pāṃsukūla).
When bedding was extremely heavy and it was difficult to carry when entering inhabited areas for business, he informed the Buddha of this matter.
The Buddha then performed a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) and permitted the making of new bedding; therefore, it is said that "except by a formal act of the Saṃgha."
Fifteenth: Once, while the Buddha was at Jetavana, on a certain day he did not accept an invitation himself but sent someone to request food.

It was the World-Honored One’s constant practice that after the bhikṣus had accepted an invitation, he would go from room to room to inspect them. There, he saw that the old sitting mats were strewn about in disorder everywhere.
The Buddha reflected on the reason for using these old items: it was for the sake of discoloring them, lest new ones be spoiled.
This was established because the color of new items is easily damaged, whereas old ones can be used as covers; and because new items are not easily damaged, this regulation was made.
Sixteenth: This originated with Upananda, who, while traveling on a road, had many sheep’s wool strands fastened to the head of his staff.
Seventeenth: Laypeople derided [the monks] like wool-shearing merchants; the Buddha heard of this and therefore established the rule.
Furthermore, it originated with the group of six bhikṣus who took wool and had the bhikṣuṇī Kautamī wash and dye it.
Because of this, she went to visit the Buddha. The Buddha saw that her hands were black and questioned the bhikṣuṇī; she answered as above. Consequently, the Buddha established the rule.

Because these bhikṣus had been prohibited from having their relatives’ nuns wash or dye their robes, the Buddha further established a rule adding the phrase "non-relatives. "Bai" (tearing) means splitting.
Eighteenth: [The rule] originated with Upananda, concerning a high minister in Rājagṛha and his friend.
He set aside some food, waiting for the Venerable One to arrive. When the minister’s son returned home from the festival festivities, he asked for food.
His mother replied that she had no other food, only that which had been set aside for Bāḷananda. She told her son to give him some money to buy food and borrow some to eat in the meantime.
When the Venerable One arrived, he heard this and, having asked for the money, departed. He then wandered among the people.
Because other bhikṣus criticized this, they reported it to the Buddha, and he therefore established a precept.
Nineteenth: He also engaged in the aforementioned practice of exchanging money for money; when laypeople saw this, they criticized him, saying, "Does this śramaṇa still exchange money for money?
Is he a skilled merchant? When the Buddha heard of this, he therefore established a precept.
Twenty: Furthermore, a certain person set out on the road and, not seeking alms, took ginger into a village to exchange it for food.
After he had departed, Śāriputra arrived later to beg for alms and went to the house where the food had been exchanged.
When the household asked for the price of the rice, Śāriputra replied, "A bhikṣu does not trade for food. They said, "It was just now that Baddhananda..."
"A bhikṣu exchanged ginger for food and departed; why, Venerable Sir, do you not exchange yours?
Furthermore, an outsider obtained a costly garment and thought to himself, "What use have I for this expensive robe? I should trade it for something else.
He then went to Jetavana, where he happened upon Baddhananda beating and washing old clothes until they looked like new ones, and so he traded with him.
A non-Buddhist, having taken refuge in another non-Buddhist sect, recognized his own [former] teacher; consequently, that non-Buddhist returned to Upananda to demand back his original robe.
Upananda would not give it back, leading to a dispute. Other bhikṣus took offense at this and reported it to the Buddha, who therefore established this rule.
21. Originating from the group of six bhikṣus who delighted in keeping fine bowls, they retained many bowls;
when the lay devotees saw this, they criticized them. The Buddha heard of it and established a prohibition. Furthermore, Ānanda obtained a bowl of high value which he wished to offer to Mahākāśyapa;
however, as Kāśyapa was away on a journey, Ānanda feared he would violate this rule. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha consequently permitted him to keep it.
22. Keeping [a bowl] for ten days.
Starting with Upananda, whose bowl was broken, he entered a city and went to the house of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*) to beg for a new bowl in exchange.
The lay devotee bought a bowl and gave it to him. In this manner, he visited many houses of lay devotees begging for bowls in exchange, and they all bought [bowls] for him.
One day, while they were together, there was another matter; the lay devotees gathered in one place and happened to speak of this.
Each of the lay devotees remarked that he had bought a bowl for him, and they all expressed their displeasure at this. When other bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha.
Therefore, the rule was established: those who wish to relinquish such bowls to the Saṃgha—specifically the many bowls requested by Upananda—should go before the Saṃgha.
The renunciation: the senior bhikṣu took the lowest bowl and gave it to Upananda; this was intended as a punishment.
(23) Furthermore, he wished to sew a saṃghāṭī for himself and entered the city to beg for thread. He begged here and there and obtained much thread, thinking to himself:
"It is difficult for a bhikṣu to obtain the three robes; I shall have someone weave them for me," and he began to do so with his own hands.
24. Because the Buddha heard that the lay devotees were resentful regarding the supervision of weaving, he established this rule.
In the city of Śrāvastī, a certain lay devotee took thread and gave it to a weaver to have a robe made as an offering for Upananda.
Having handed the thread to the weaver, he departed. The weaver then took the thread and went to the Jeta Grove to report [the matter].
Bhadrananda gave instructions to a skilled weaver to produce a cloth that was wide, long, and of fine quality. The weaver said, "There is not enough thread.
Nanda then went to the householder’s home and requested more thread for the weaver. The weaver further remarked, "The wages are too low.
Nanda said, "I shall increase your payment. When the householder returned from his travels, his wife asked him about the previous matter.
The formal motion (*jñapti*) was as stated above. Because of his resentment toward this, other bhikṣus heard of it and reported it to the Buddha;
therefore, he established this rule. (25) Venerable Nanda had a disciple who was skilled at exhorting and converting others.
Upananda was pleased with him and made an agreement to travel together through the human world. Because of a dispute over a robe, another bhikṣu spoke privately to the disciple regarding Upananda.
Upananda acted contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya, transgressing many precepts; one should not associate with him. His disciple, however, refused him and would not let him go.

Upananda became angry and seized back the robe he had given. He then raised his voice, and when the bhikṣus in the neighboring rooms asked for the reason [for the commotion], they reported it to the Buddha. Consequently, the Buddha established this rule.
26. At that time, in the autumn month at Jetavana, the bhikṣus suffered from wind-related illnesses, sores, and scabies.

The Buddha permitted them to take five kinds of medicinal substances. Previously, he had prohibited eating at improper times (vikālabhojana); thus, although they now possessed the medicines, they did not dare to take them at improper times.
Consequently, their illnesses were not cured. Thereupon, he further permitted sick bhikṣus to take medicine both at proper and improper times.
When the Buddha was traveling through the borders of the kingdom of Magadha with one thousand two hundred and fifty followers, Pindola Bharadvaja had resided in this city for a long time;
those who knew him well provided him with great offerings, and his disciples accumulated vast stores of provisions.
The lay devotees took offense at this, and when the Buddha heard of it, he established a prohibition.
27. In the city of Śrāvastī, the upāsikā Viśākhā prepared a meal to offer to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
She sent her maidservant to Jetavana to announce that the time had come. At that moment, it was raining heavily.

The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to bathe in the rain; they all bathed naked in the rain. The maidservant caught sight of them and returned to inform her mistress. After the meal, [the Buddha addressed the assembly:]...
Śakra addressed the Buddha, requesting that he grant the Sangha the gift of rain-bathing robes (*varṣāśāṭī*). Consequently, the Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to keep rain-season robes.
Later, the group of six bhikṣus (*ṣaḍvargika*) began to beg for these robes during the spring, summer, and winter seasons. The other bhikṣus took offense at this and reported it to the Buddha;
thus, the rule was established: "When one month of spring remains" refers to the sixteenth day of the third month. That...
The year is divided into three seasons; therefore, one should seek rain and use the bathing robes starting from the sixteenth day of the third month until the first day of the fourth month.
If one seeks rain or uses the robes before these dates, both constitute an offense.
28. At that time, there was a rebellion among the people in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. The King dispatched a high minister to suppress it.
The minister thought to himself, "The bhikṣus have not yet completed their summer retreat; ten days still remain.

Since I am now departing for the campaign and will not be able to return, I should first offer robes and provide offerings. Consequently, he went to the Jeta Grove and invited the bhikṣus at his pleasure, saying, "I shall simply provide the offerings."

While the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) had not yet concluded, he did not dare to accept the robes; he reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha permitted him to accept "urgent offering robes" (*ātyayika-cīvara*) and allowed them to be kept until the time for [regular] robes.
(29) According to that land, one year is divided into three seasons, each lasting four months; this is what is stated in the present text.

Regarding the "three months of summer," these three months constitute the formal rule for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). The remaining one month is set aside as an interval for preparing robes and traveling.
Based on this, the retreat begins on the sixteenth day of the fourth month and concludes on the fifteenth day of the seventh month;
thus, because one month remains, it is said that the period is "fulfilled" on the fifteenth day of the eighth month. As for the phrase "extremely distant," etc., it is due to... [text ends].
While other bhikṣus were completing their rains retreat dwelling in an araṇya, they were robbed of their robes, sitting mats, needle-cases, and various requisites by bandits;

furthermore, the bandits beat some of the bhikṣus. Out of fear of the bandits, they all came to reside at Jetavana. Consequently, the Buddha established a further regulation (as detailed in the text).
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had permitted staying overnight separated from one's robes, so they deposited their robes [with others].
A monk who had entrusted his robes to another went away on a journey among the people and did not return for a long time.

The monk who held the deposit was drying the robes at midday when another monk learned of this and reported it to the Buddha. Consequently, a further restriction was established: [the period of custody] shall be limited to six days; anyone exceeding this limit commits an offense.
30. A householder in the city of Śrāvastī wished to provide offerings and robes.

When he went to Jetavana to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha, Upāli (Bhadanta) arrived at his house first and said, "The community of bhikṣus will all be satisfied; there is no need to prepare everything.
You need not provide full sets of food and clothing for the entire Saṃgha; you may simply give the robes to me alone. The householder believed him and consequently failed to make the preparations.
The next day, when it was time for the Buddha and the community of monks to go to the house of that lay devotee, the layperson saw the dignified deportment and venerable reputation of the bhikṣus;
he regretted not having prepared the robes and, upon recounting the incident involving Upananda, [the Buddha] established this rule.
This concludes the thirty preceding *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules.

○ Ninety *pāyattika* Dharmas: The Sanskrit term *pāyattika* is translated here as "falling back" (*duòqián*). This refers to the punishment for offenses regarding robes and bowls, wherein one must forfeit (*shè*) the object;
hence it is called "forfeiture and falling" (*shěduò*). However, these ninety rules herein involve punishment for conduct and speech where there is nothing to forfeit;
therefore, they are simply termed "falling" (*duò*). "Falling" (*duò*) means to incur a loss or defeat. There are [two types of] falling...
Because they commit a fallen offense:
first, having engaged in debate with the Venerable Hatthipada of the Śākya clan— who was highly skilled in discussion—
whenever he encountered a point in the debate that he could not overcome among the śramaṇas or brahmins, he would reverse his previous argument and speak falsely despite knowing the truth.
The Saṃgha took offense at this and informed the Buddha, who therefore established the rule.
Second, it originated when the group of six bhikṣus, while settling a dispute, insulted and reviled a bhikṣu by calling him a member of a low and base caste, causing him shame;
for this reason, the rule was established.
Third, it was established because the six groups of monks (ṣaḍvargika) initiated conversations in private with one another, causing disputes to persist; therefore, the rule was enacted.
Fourth, it originated from the Venerable Aniruddha, who, while traveling along a remote road, arrived at a place where no bhikṣus were residing.
While traveling through a village seeking lodging, the Venerable One stayed overnight at the house of a courtesan.
As he was spreading out his bedding within the room, another elder also arrived seeking lodging and stayed in the same room as the Venerable One.
When the elder’s many servants crowded close to the Venerable One, the courtesan took pity on him and said, "In my room..."
Regarding the Venerable One who had previously attained non-exaltation: how was it that he stayed in the same room as a courtesan until the final watch of the night?
When the courtesan’s lustful desire arose, she spoke of this matter to the Venerable One. The Venerable One, with right concentration manifest before him, remained silent and did not answer.
She then removed her clothes and desired to draw near to him; however, the Venerable One leaped his body into the air, and the courtesan was filled with shame.
Feeling ashamed, he joined his palms and requested absolution; this was repeated three times. The Venerable One returned to his original seat.
Once back at the Jeta Grove, he recounted these events as they had occurred, and the Buddha consequently established this precept.
Fifth: When the Buddha was at the city of Khāṇumata, one among the group of six bhikṣus [interacted] with several elders.
While staying together in this monastery, a monk fell into a deep sleep and rolled over naked. His neighbor, seeing him, covered him with his robe;
however, after a short while, he was exposed again. Those who were lying with him mocked and teased him.

When the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule for the bhikṣus, prohibiting them from staying overnight with those who had not yet received the full ordination. Rāhula was the son of the Buddha.
A novice who had not yet received the full precepts was sent out of his room; having nowhere else to go, he stayed overnight in the latrine.
The Buddha, seeing this with his divine eye, went to the latrine, led him back to his own quarters, and stayed there with him for one night.
The next day, he rebuked the monks for their lack of compassion in driving the young child out, and subsequently established the rule that they must stay for two or three nights.

Sixth: Furthermore, because the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) rose together with various elders to recite Buddhist sūtras, their voices disturbing those in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), [the Buddha] established this regulation.
Seventh: When the Buddha was at Vulture Peak Mountain (*Gṛdhrakūṭaparvata*), there were bhikṣus practicing *parivāsa* and *mānatva*.
Those [monks] were sitting in the lower row; the group of six bhikṣus pointed to those bhikṣus in the lower row and spoke to the laypeople, saying, "So many people are sitting in the lower row.
Because this constitutes a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), they caused them to sit in the lower row.
When those bhikṣus in the lower row heard this, they felt ashamed and reproached the group of six, and consequently informed the Buddha, who therefore established this rule.

Regarding the exception for *saṃgha-karman*: at one time, Śāriputra was appointed by the assembly to inform the kings, ministers, elders, and lay devotees of Devadatta’s schism and other rebellious acts. Fearing that he might violate this precept, Śāriputra informed the Buddha;
the Buddha granted him *karman*, and thus established the exception for *saṃgha-karman* so that there would be no offense.
Eighth: While residing at the Pārileyyaka Garden, there was a bhikṣu who spoke of superhuman attainments to various śrāmaṇeras and householders;
the Buddha heard of this and therefore established the prohibition.
Ninth: Kāḷudāyin entered a certain elder’s house in Śrāvastī and, while standing before his mother-in-law, spoke the Dharma into the ear of her daughter-in-law.
The mother-in-law said, "When preaching the Dharma, one should speak loudly so that we may hear;
why do you speak only into the ear? When the Buddha heard this, he established this precept for all women thereafter.
When the Blessed One requested the bhikṣus to preach the Dharma, the bhikṣus did not dare to do so.
He informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha permitted them to preach the Dharma to women for five or six sentences. If they exceed five or six sentences, it constitutes an offense;
however, if a wise man is present before the woman while preaching the Dharma, exceeding that limit does not constitute an offense. For this reason, it is said that [the rule] is "excepted."
Tenth: It originated when the group of six bhikṣus personally dug the earth while repairing a lecture hall for the Buddha;
because the local elders complained that digging with one's own hands harms the lives of insects, the Buddha heard of this and established the prohibition.
11. Originating from the case of the monk Kalandaka, who cut down a tree with his own hand— since all trees, grasses, and shrubs are the abodes of spirits (*bhūta*),
cutting down a tree is called "destroying a village of spirits" because it deprives them of their dwelling— the Buddha heard of this and established the prohibition.

12. Originating with the Bhikṣu Cunda: When a bhikṣu who had committed an offense was questioned by those administering the disciplinary procedure, saying, "Do you know whether you have committed this offense?", he deliberately evaded the question and did not answer correctly. The Buddha heard of this and therefore established the rule.
13. When the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra arose, the Venerable Sthavira Śāriputra knew that the saṃgha’s seating mats and food were being provided for him.
Maitrāyaṇīputra spoke of the Venerable’s partiality and aversion in a secluded place. When the other bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked Maitrāyaṇīputra.
Maitrāyaṇīputra replied, "I was merely expressing my displeasure in a secluded place," yet he continued to harbor such displeasure afterward.
The monks did not cease their severe reproaches. He replied, "I do not despise you; I was merely reviling you. When this was reported to the Buddha, he therefore established the rule.
(14) At that time, when a meal was being prepared by a householder in the city of Śrāvastī for the Saṃgha, the time arrived for the group of seventeen monks.
When a bhikṣu took a monastic sitting mat and spread it out in the open air to sit upon, he departed without withdrawing it when the time came;

consequently, it was defiled by wind-blown dust and crows. Because the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule. As for the "group of seventeen," those who were between twelve and seventeen years of age constituted one class, and thus they were called the "group of seventeen."
15. At that time, a visiting bhikṣu in Jeta’s Grove said to a resident bhikṣu, “I have spread my bedding and stayed overnight in a remote room;
later, without informing you, I departed without putting it away, and the bedding has become rotten.
The resident bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, who therefore established the rule.

The group of seventeen said to the group of six, "Venerable sirs, you go on ahead to seek a place to stay for the night.
The group of six replied, "What business is that of yours? You all go on ahead! At that time, the group of seventeen went first to seek lodging and prepared it in advance.
Regarding bedding: the group of six monks arrived later and forcibly spread their bedding within it (and so forth). Other bhikṣus took offense at this and informed the Buddha;
therefore, he established this rule.

29. At that time, a householder in the city of Śrāvastī invited Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana to a meal.
