The Master first intended not to commit [an offense].
Thirty. When Anuruddha arose, a woman of Vaiśālī married a man from Śrāvastī;
she quarreled with her mother-in-law and secretly returned to her own country. At that time, Anuruddha was traveling from Śrāvastī toward Vaiśālī.
In a town outside the city, a woman asked the Venerable One for his belt so she might go with him; the Venerable One consented and traveled together with her.
Later, her husband pursued them and rebuked Ānanda, asking, "What kind of man are you, that you take another's wife and flee?
When Ānanda explained the matter, he did not believe him and beat the Venerable One until he was near death; the Venerable One endured it while remaining on the path below.
Sitting cross-legged, he entered the *ābhāsvara-samādhi*. The man was moved by compassion and turned toward virtue, repenting before the Venerable One.
Having accepted his repentance, the Venerable One departed. Upon returning to the Jeta Grove, he recounted the matter himself, and the Buddha consequently established a precept.

31. At that time, a householder of the Kosalā country was constructing a dwelling where none had previously existed to provide hospitality for the Saṃgha, stipulating only that they receive a single meal.
The group of six bhikṣus went there, obtained excellent food and drink, and remained for a long time without departing.
The householders resented this, and other bhikṣus informed the Buddha. Consequently, he established this precept as a śaikṣa rule.
When the Buddha was at Vaiśālī, he did not dare to eat excessively while ill, and as he departed supported by his illness, the ailment subsequently grew more severe.
The Buddha, becoming aware of this, consequently established a precept that those who are not ill shall incur an offense for eating excessively.

32. While the Buddha was traveling through the territory of the Aṇāpinḍada country with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, there was a śramaṇa brāhmaṇa who followed behind the Buddha in a carriage carrying food and drink.
He intended to provide a meal for the assembly on days when no offerings were received; as time passed, he did not fail to provide offerings on a single day.
He said to Ānanda, "My original intention was that my current offerings were insufficient;

having been away from home for a long time, I wish to spread the goods I have loaded onto my cart upon the road so that the Buddha and the Sangha may tread upon them as an act of worship, after which I shall depart.
Ānanda stayed behind on his behalf and informed the Buddha. The Buddha commanded that gruel be prepared for the assembly of monks.
After eating congee, they then proceeded to the invitations. When the various householders heard this, they would prepare congee and send it to the monks' quarters before the invitations;
on the day a high minister provided an offering, the bhikṣus first ate fine congee and then ate very little at the minister's house.
The minister took offense at this and reported it to the Buddha. Therefore, the rule was established: [one must not eat the meal provided by the host before having eaten the congee].
Regarding the rules on eating in succession (*paryāya-bhojana*), the various underlying causes and conditions for each instance are too numerous to record in full.

(33) At that time, Devadatta incited others to harm the Buddha; as his ill repute spread and his offerings and gains were cut off, he went with his faction—Devadatta and the others—to beg for food from house to house, which is called "eating apart from the community" (*gaṇa-bhojana*).

Once this precept was established, sick bhikṣus who had been invited to a meal did not dare to eat separately from the assembly. Consequently, the Buddha further instituted a regulation to exclude these "exceptional times.
Regarding "the time for making robes": this refers to the period when a bhikṣu, having completed the *pravāraṇā*, is engaged in preparing robes.

Regarding "the time for the distribution of robes": this refers to when a donor bestows robes while also providing offerings; hence it is called "the time for the distribution of robes. Furthermore, it concerns when a bhikṣu [is with] his companions...
While traveling on a long journey, a companion went to beg for food midway along the way. His companion said, "Eat with us. The bhikṣu replied, "I dare not eat separately from the community.
Because of this, he entered the village to beg for food while his companion had already gone on ahead; the bhikṣu was subsequently robbed by bandits.
Therefore, it was permitted to eat separately from the community while traveling on the road. The same applies when traveling by boat. Furthermore, regarding King Bimbisāra:
34. A sister-in-law named Kālī wished to hold a great assembly to provide food for the śramaṇas; however, the bhikṣus did not dare to attend the meal.
For this reason, they informed the Buddha, who consequently permitted the holding of meals during a great assembly.
At that time, there was a woman from a large village in Śrāvastī who had married a man from the country of Ujjayinī and had returned to her parents' home to visit them.
While a man was preparing food with right faith to give to a mendicant bhikṣu, his wife’s family arrived to take her back home. She said, "I have finished cooking;
let us go together to beg for alms. As the monks arrived one after another, she could not leave. The husband became angry and took another wife.
Later, a merchant prepared food along the road, and when a mendicant bhikṣu arrived, he divided his own food and gave it to him before departing.
When the alms-seeking monks arrived again, they divided [the food] and departed; once their own portions were exhausted, they prepared more.
Their companions who had gone there earlier were subsequently plundered by bandits. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, and thus he established this precept.
However, because sick bhikṣus did not dare to accept food beyond the limit, the Buddha further prescribed the rule regarding those who are not ill.
35. While the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, he taught the monks the practice of eating a single meal in one sitting and praised this method of eating a single meal.
Upon hearing this, the monks adopted the practice of eating a single meal; because they did not eat again, their bodies became emaciated.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "For what reason have the monks become so emaciated? Ānanda answered as above. Thereupon, the Buddha permitted [the practice].

The bhikṣus, having already eaten their fill while seated on a single mat, did not dare to eat again even when they encountered the five kinds of fine foods and medicinal herbs, as their bodies remained emaciated.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, and Ānanda replied as before. The Buddha further permitted the Saṃgha to eat the five kinds of food.
These five kinds of food are: boiled rice, parched grain flour, dried cakes, and other pure meats. Regarding these five kinds...
To ensure that all sick bhikṣus were satisfied, the Buddha permitted that they could not be satiated in a single sitting;
furthermore, they were not allowed to eat again from the remaining food. The Buddha further authorized the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the practice of leftover food). Regarding the *khalupaścādbhakti*:
if a bhikṣu has already finished his meal and receives more food, that bhikṣu should eat a small amount and say to another bhikṣu, "Eat as you please."
Taking food in this manner is called the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the practice of leftover food). If one eats again without having performed the *khalupaścādbhakti*, one commits an offense.
(36) In Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who was greedy for food and never felt satisfied.
Other bhikṣus spoke of his gluttony in this way. That bhikṣu, harboring shame and resentment in his heart, later encountered some food on another occasion.
That gluttonous bhikṣu, having not performed the *kṛtāvadhi* (the ritual for leftover food), earnestly urged the one who spoke before him to eat;
that speaker then accepted the food. The gluttonous bhikṣu likewise thought that the one who spoke before him was gluttonous and felt a sense of shame toward that person.
The bhikṣu who had received the food asked: "Do you know that I have already eaten my fill?"
"Furthermore, you urged me to eat. That bhikṣu replied, "Indeed, indeed; knowing that I had already finished my meal, you urged me, thereby causing me to commit an offense.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and thus [the rule] was established.
37. At that time, during a festival in the city of Rājagṛha, various musical performances were being held.
The two bhikṣus, Nanda and Upananda, went to watch them. The laypeople said to one another, "You are watching in vain;
you should provide food and drink for these two bhikṣus. Those people then gave them food and drink together. After the two bhikṣus had eaten, they watched the performance.
As evening approached, the bhikṣus returned to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and asked why they had not returned until so late.
The two bhikṣus explained the matter to them. Furthermore, on another occasion, Kālodāyin went out for alms at dusk;
a pregnant woman opened her door and, suddenly seeing him, was startled, thinking he was a ghost, and consequently miscarried. The Buddha heard of this incident and established a rule.
38. At Vulture Peak, when the Venerable Kāla was going for alms, he thought: "What is the use of begging for food every day and entering the city?
It causes me emaciation and suffering. From now on, I shall set aside what remains from today's meal for tomorrow, and what remains from tomorrow's for the day after.
Consequently, the monks did not see Kāla during either the morning or the midday meal.
Because Rāhula inquired and learned of this, he reported it to the Blessed One, and thus [the rule] was established.
(39) At that time, a certain bhikṣu in Jeta’s Grove had this thought: "I shall always beg for alms and wear rag-robes from refuse heaps.
He then set out on this practice. While begging for alms, he saw men and women by a river or in a city...
If one prepares food for the sacrifice of deceased ancestors and a bhikṣu takes and eats it without receiving it from another person, this is called "taking food without having received it.
When the person performing the sacrifice saw this, he spoke with resentment, saying, "The bhikṣu took and ate the food without being given it.

The Buddha heard of this and therefore established the rule: if medicine is placed within the mouth—meaning whatever there may be, whether clarified butter (sarpis) or parched grain flour (maṇḍa)—[it is considered taken].
40. It is an offense to take medicine that has not been offered and place it in one's mouth.
At that time, the Venerable Upananda had previously had a merchant as a donor.
When it was time for him to go on his alms round, he went to the merchant’s house and said, "I wish to eat various fine foods; please prepare them for me. The merchant asked:
The merchant asked, "What affliction do you have, Bhikṣu? The Bhikṣu replied, "I have no affliction.
The merchant said, "If you have no affliction, Bhikṣu, why do you still long for fine food? We merchants endure great toil and hardship, yet we do not even obtain fine food to eat.
When other bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the World-Honored One, and thus [the rule] was established.
41. While the Buddha and the bhikṣus were traveling from the country of Kosala toward Śrāvastī, various donors along the way made offerings of a great quantity of cakes.
The Buddha instructed Ānanda to distribute the cakes among the community of monks.
When there was a remainder, the Buddha instructed that it be distributed to the beggars. Among the beggars was a naked female ascetic (nirgranthī) of beautiful countenance.
When the portion of the cake was being distributed, two cakes stuck together; Ānanda did not notice and divided them for the girl.
When those nearby questioned him and learned that the girl had received two, they said that Ānanda had feelings for her.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who therefore established the rule.
42. In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a householder who invited the bhikṣu-saṃgha along with Upananda for a meal.
When the saṃgha had assembled, Upananda went to another house to eat. The time for the meal had already arrived, yet he had not yet returned.
The bhikṣus requested food, and the householder said, "Wait until Upananda arrives. The bhikṣus replied, "The time for the meal has passed."

The food was insufficient. Furthermore, a certain lay devotee sent a messenger with fresh fruit to the Jeta Grove to provide for the Sangha, instructing the messenger to wait until after Baddhananda had finished his portion.
That day, Baddhananda went to another house and did not return until mealtime had passed, so that the assembly of monks was unable to eat the fresh fruit. They reported this matter to the Buddha.

Regarding the restriction concerning other times: there are causes and conditions as previously explained; when one goes to another's house and entrusts the matter to another bhikṣu, it is because one has instructed the person so that they may know [of the situation], and thus one eats without waiting [for the host].
43. Beginning with Kālodayin’s visit to the house of a laywoman observing the uposatha:
when the wife of that layman offered food to the Venerable One, he ate for a long time and did not leave. Her husband repeatedly sent him away, yet he would not go.
The husband resented this, and the Buddha heard of it; therefore, he established the rule regarding "jewels," which includes gold, silver, and other such items.
44. Also because he rose from his seat and sat in a secluded place at the house of the upāsikā Cīrṇadhyaya.
45. Also because that person was likewise from that same family.
46. Udāyin, having previously fought with a certain bhikṣu and wishing to offer him an act of reconciliation, harbored resentment in his heart;
he therefore invited that monk into the city to provide him with food. As they traveled about the entire city, when the time for the meal arrived, he did not give him any food and sent him away.
That bhikṣu entered the Jeta Grove without having received any food, as Udāyin had dismissed him.
47. Having gone to a family for a meal and returned after having eaten his fill, the Buddha heard of this and therefore established the rule.
While the Buddha was staying in Kapilavastu, Mahānāma of the Śākya clan provided medicinal herbs to the community of monks;
out of respect for the senior elder, he gave excellent medicine whether asked or unasked. Among the group of six, they [acted] toward one another...
"We shall go to that house to seek [medicine]," they said. When they arrived and were seeking it, by chance they lacked medicine and had to purchase it elsewhere.
The six clansmen scolded them, saying, "Your house has no medicine; how can you provide for the Sangha? You harbor likes and dislikes, and moreover, you speak falsely.
Śreṇika Bimbisāra replied, "I previously made a vow: 'If there is medicine in the house, I shall provide it; if not, I shall purchase it and give it.'"

He said, "I am mistaken; I shall no longer provide medicine for the Saṃgha. Because other bhikṣus were displeased with the Ṣaḍvargika monks for falsely rebuking him and causing him to cease providing medicinal requisites for the Saṃgha, they informed the World-Honored One. Consequently, the Buddha established a rule permitting the Saṃgha to receive medicine for four months.
"Four months" refers to one of the three seasons. At that time, the sick bhikṣu had exceeded the four-month period.
I venture to further receive from the Buddha the renewed regulation that one who is not ill and accepts [medicine] commits an offense.

Furthermore, there was a householder who regularly invited [monks] to receive medicine, yet Śreṇika Bimbisāra invited them again to provide medicine; there were also those who offered invitations for specific occasions and those who offered lifelong support.
Because the Buddha permitted the acceptance of all these, [the previous rule] is thus excluded (and so forth).
48. At that time, King Prasenajit was on a military expedition. The group of six monks went to observe him, and the King became displeased with them.

He entrusted a bag of honey to the World-Honored One as an offering. Because the Buddha had sent the group of six monks to observe [the King], he subsequently established the rule concerning military commanders;
the name of the general was Rishidatta. When he wished to see a bhikṣu, he dispatched a messenger to invite the World-Honored One, and the Buddha granted permission.
49. Formerly, there was no offense for those who went [to the army] except under specific causes and conditions.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus had business and stayed overnight in the midst of an army; those who saw this disparaged them.
Other bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and he therefore established the rule.

Fifty: At one time, the group of six monks stayed overnight among the troops on some business; while watching a battle, one monk was struck by an arrow and returned carried on a litter wrapped in his robes.
When people questioned this, the assembly all looked upon it with disapproval. The Buddha heard of this and therefore established a regulation.
51. The account beginning with the Venerable Sāgata, who was formerly among the group of six, seeking lodging at the house of a certain brahmin.
The brahmin said, "There is an empty room, but I cannot allow you to stay there. The Venerable asked, "For what reason? He replied, "Because there is a venomous dragon within;
I fear it might harm you. The Venerable said, "Just let me stay; it will do no harm," and he immediately spread out his seat.
Having sat down, at midnight a venomous dragon saw that the monks were staying there and spat forth fire and smoke.

Sāgata entered the fire-element concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) and likewise emitted fire; the dragon became exceedingly enraged and let loose a great blaze, and Sāgata also released a great fire.
As they burned each other, Sāgata thought, "I shall extinguish that poisonous fire," and the dragon's flames gradually subsided.
The fire of the *gāthā* blazed even more fiercely, whereupon he subdued that nāga and placed it within his alms-bowl.

On the following day, when he showed [the nāga] to the brahmin, the King of Kauśāmbī happened to be at the brahmin’s house. Having developed faith and reverence for the Venerable One, he had previously instructed the brahmin:
"If the Venerable One comes again, inform me so that I may provide him with a single offering. At another time, Sagada returned once more to the brahmin’s house.
The brahmin replied to the king, who had personally invited the group of six bhikṣus, saying: "It is easy for you to preach to the king;
what is difficult to obtain is the provision of offerings for the bhikṣus. The king asked, "What is difficult to obtain?
He replied, "Only black liquor is difficult to obtain. When the time arrived the following day, Sāgata went to the king's residence, where various kinds [of offerings] were prepared.
Having overeaten fine food and drunk strong liquor, he became intoxicated upon returning; he fell to the ground and vomited, and crows and magpies ate the vomit while cawing chaotically.
The Buddha knew this and intentionally questioned Ānanda, who reported the matter in full as above. The Buddha said, "Foolish man!
Formerly you could subdue great dragons, yet now you cannot even subdue a small snake. Therefore, he established this precept.

52. At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus were bathing and playing in the waters of the Ajiravatī River, moving with and against the current, submerging and emerging, and tossing themselves about.
King Bimbisāra and Queen Mallikā, looking down from a high tower, saw them. The King and the Queen conversed: "These young ones have gone forth into the Buddha-dharma..."

Because it was profound, the Blessed One descended from the upper story of the palace and dispatched the Brahmin Nālanda to deliver his greetings to the World-Honored One, reporting this matter in full;
thus the rule was established.
(53) Among the group of six, one struck with a wooden block against a member of the group of seventeen until he died; others were likewise [struck].

54. The Buddha established this rule because [the monks] informed him of what had occurred. It originated with the bhikṣu Chanda, who wished to violate the precepts; although the other bhikṣus admonished him, he did not comply, so they informed the Buddha, and thus it was established.
55. While the Buddha was walking up and down on his walking path in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, the Venerable Nāgapāla attended upon him at his side.
During the first watch of the night, he requested the Buddha to return to his chamber; this continued until the middle watch and the last watch, when the sky was about to break into dawn.
The Buddha still had not returned. Nāgapāla thought to himself: "I have requested him repeatedly, yet he does not return; I must now be concerned."
56. Frightening him so that he would return, [the monk] instead put on coarse clothing and made a terrifying sound; the Buddha could not frighten him.
After the Buddha had admonished him, he established a rule. 57.
When the Buddha was in Magadha, there was a king who possessed hot springs which he constantly provided for the Sangha to bathe in. At that time, six... [monks]... (The text is incomplete).
Later in the night, while a group of bhikṣus were bathing, the King arrived with his court ladies to bathe as well.

Hearing that the Saṃgha was bathing, he ordered them not to be startled and waited until their bath was finished. The group of six bhikṣus bathed for so long that it reached dawn, yet they did not leave; consequently, the King was unable to bathe at all and departed.
For this reason, [the Buddha] established the rule: "When it is extremely hot, [bathing is permitted] for a bhikṣu who is afflicted by a disease involving filth..."
57. During a journey in wind and rain, one may not bathe; because this was reported to the Buddha, he further established a rule permitting [bathing] at other times.
58. It originated with the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) when the Buddha was in the city of Kalandaka.
The group of six said to one another, "We cannot speak as we please in the presence of the elders," and they immediately went out from their rooms onto the open ground to gather [things].
While burning wild wood to warm his body, he did not realize that a venomous snake was hidden within a decaying tree.

As the smoke from the fire permeated the interior, the snake was startled and fled headlong; the six groups of monks, fleeing in panic, scattered the burning logs, causing them to spread and set the lecture hall on fire.
For this reason, it was subsequently prohibited. Furthermore, due to the illness of bhikṣus and various other circumstances, none dared to burn fire thereafter.
Exclusion.
58. While the Buddha was at Jetavana, there was a householder who invited the monks for a meal.

At that time, the seventeen groups of bhikṣus took their robes and bowls, hung them to one side, and practiced walking meditation (caṅkrama) at the walking path, waiting for the appointed hour. The six groups of bhikṣus...
While playing, Kṣemaka hid another monk’s robe; when he heard it was time for the announcement, he searched for the robe but could not find it.

The group of six monks had hidden the robe, and when the other monks saw this, they reported it. Because the group of six monks had playfully hidden it, the Buddha consequently established the precept.
59. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus first gave their robes to others and later took them back and wore them without asking the original owners.
The Buddha heard of this and established a rule prohibiting it.
60. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore new white robes, which the laypeople disliked. The Buddha, on account of this, established a rule.
61. Regarding the three colors—blue, black, and madder—it is because these three colors are applied interchangeably, rather than being exclusively blue, black, or madder.
This [incident] originated with Kāḷudāyin, who, being displeased by the sound of a crow, shot it dead with a bow.
62. Because various householders criticized and disparaged [the monks], and the Buddha heard of it, he established this rule.
63. It originated with the group of six [monks] who took water containing mixed insects, whether for drinking or for use; because householders saw this and were displeased, he established this rule.
63. The Seventeen Groups of Bhikṣus Ask the Six Groups of Bhikṣus about the Dharmas of the Various Dhyānas and the Four Fruits.

The Six Groups replied, "You have spoken falsely regarding the attainment of the state of a superior person; you have committed a *pārājika* offense. The Seventeen Groups went to the Elder and asked him separately.
The Elder reported, "There is no offense," and he informed the Buddha of this matter. Consequently, the rule was established.
64. Udāyin was intimate with a certain monk. Udāyin repeatedly committed offenses and said to his intimate friend, "I have committed such-and-such an offense; do not speak of it to others.
Later, he quarreled with that intimate monk, who immediately spoke of it to other monks. When the Saṃgha questioned him, [Udāyin] asked, "When did this happen?"
65. When the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, there were seventeen groups of lay youths in the city of Rājagṛha;
the eldest was seventeen years old and the youngest was twelve. Among them were both the wealthy and the poor.
Because [a monk] had committed an offense and concealed it until now, he informed the Buddha of this matter, and thus [the rule] was established.
When they encouraged one another with the desire to seek ordination, the bhikṣus ordained them, granting them the full precepts (upasampadā).
Because these youths were so young and unaccustomed to training, they could not endure eating only one meal; at midnight, suffering from hunger, they wailed aloud.
The Buddha, knowing this, questioned Ānanda, who replied as stated above; therefore, [the Buddha] established the rule.
66. At that time, because the six groups of bhikṣus had already settled a dispute but then provoked it again, [the Buddha] established this rule.
67. When many bhikṣus were about to go to the city of Vaiśālī from Jetavana, there was a merchant who wished to evade customs duties and invited the Saṃgha to travel with him.
Upon arriving at the customs post, they were seized by the customs officers according to the law of the customs.
68. When King Prasenajit issued an edict that those who evade taxes should be put to death, the Buddha heard of this and established the rule for the monks.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Ariṣṭa in Jeta’s Grove who held such evil views; although the other bhikṣus admonished him three times, he would not desist.
The Buddha heard of this and established the rule.

69. Furthermore, because the six groups of monks (Ṣaḍvargika) still provided for, stayed with, performed formal acts (karmavācanā) together with, and conversed with that aforementioned person who did not relinquish his evil views, the Blessed One ordained this [rule] by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).

70. At that time, in Jeta’s Grove, the two śrāmaṇeras of Bāḍhananda—one named Kana and the other named Mahuka—engaged in unchaste conduct together and spoke to one another as follows (as detailed). The bhikṣus, disapproving of these two śrāmaṇeras, reported this matter to the Buddha.
Consequently, the Buddha established the rule for "exclusion" (*pravāsanīya-karman*); thus, the act of exclusion was performed against them, and they were banished to a distance.

It was because he had departed after erasing his tracks; at that time, the group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) enticed and harbored animals for them to stay overnight, and thus it was ordained in this manner.
(71) At that time, the bhikṣu Channa, when other bhikṣus admonished him in accordance with the Dharma, spoke in response as follows: "I myself..."

72. Furthermore, because the Buddha heard that those who did not study the precepts yet wished to rebuke other bhikṣus, he established this regulation; however, he made an exception for one who asks about the characteristics of the precepts while seeking to understand them with difficulty, as such a person does not commit an offense.
At that time, many bhikṣus were teaching the Dharma and reciting the precepts in one place at Jetavana, while the group of six bhikṣus...
The Buddha saw them reciting the precepts and said to one another, "They are proficient in reciting the precepts and frequently come forward to raise charges against us;
we shall stop them and need not recite these trivial rules of minor detail.

If one wishes to recite, it is sufficient to recite the four *pārājika* offenses and the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. (And so forth. Because they reported this to the Buddha, he established the rule.
73. When the Buddha was at Jeta’s Grove, there was one bhikṣu among the group of six who knew he had committed an offense.
At the time of the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), he intentionally feigned ignorance in order to avoid being accused of his transgression.

The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and consequently, the rule was established to further increase the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*): in addition to the punishment for the actual offense committed, another offense of ignorance was added.
74. At that time, because the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin was occupied with monastic affairs and had no leisure to accept invitations from outside, his robes became worn and torn.
As the other bhikṣus frequently accepted invitations from outside and obtained costly robes on a single day, they all resolved to give them to the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin.
Consequently, he formally requested the Saṃgha for a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) in accordance with the Dharma.
When giving [a robe], the group of six monks intentionally made this remark: "Give the robe to the monk who is a relative.
When the other bhikṣus heard this, they censured them and reported it to the Buddha;

therefore, he established this rule. (75) At that time, when the assembly of monks had gathered in Jeta’s Grove and were about to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*), the group of six [monks] themselves...

This means that when they said, "If you intend to expose our transgressions, it would be better for you to leave first so that your accusation does not succeed," and having said this, they immediately departed, the bhikṣus said to them, "Do not go;
have you gone because there is some business? They reported this matter to the Buddha, and thus he established the rule.
76. At that time, among the group of six in Jeta’s Grove, there was one who had committed an offense.
Fearing that the Saṃgha would bring him to account, he followed his own faction. When the Saṃgha saw their violent behavior, they temporarily desisted.
Later, while the group of six was making robes, the Saṃgha took the opportunity to summon them on another matter. They replied, "We are busy making robes and have no leisure. Thus they were summoned.
It is said that if there were no leisure, one or two people could be sent to carry the *chanda* (consent) away and thus conclude the matter;

however, because one or two people were subsequently sent and the assembly was informed to proceed with the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), the person later refused to comply, leading to further reproach; therefore, the rule was established.
77. At that time, because the group of six bhikṣus incited mutual strife and discord so as to prevent disputes from being settled, [the Buddha] established this rule.
78. Because one person among the group of six became angry and struck a member of the group of seventeen, [the Buddha] established this rule.
79. Because the group of six bhikṣus, out of anger, struck and throttled the group of seventeen bhikṣus—"struck" here meaning to seize and throttle—the [rule] was established.
80. Also because the group of six bhikṣus, out of anger, falsely slandered and insulted the group of seventeen bhikṣus, it was established.
81. Once, when Kāḷudāyin had entered King Prasenajit’s palace, the king and Queen Mallikā were sleeping together during the day and had not yet risen.
When the Queen saw the Venerable from afar, she immediately rose, put on her robe, and prepared a seat for him to sit upon.
The Queen lost her garment, which fell to the ground; consequently, she remained crouching and did not rise, while Kāḷudāyin [remained seated].
The Venerable One immediately departed from the palace and returned to the Jeta Grove, where he recounted the aforementioned events. Upon hearing this, the Buddha established the rule for Kṣatriyas.
"Kṣatriya" is a term of Sanskrit origin; in full it is *Kṣatriya*, which means "royal lineage. Regarding those who are "anointed with water":

when a Wheel-Turning King first succeeds to his station, a golden pitcher filled with the waters of the four great oceans is brought, and the King personally holds the pitcher to pour the water over the crown of the Prince's head.

He is called "Anointed with Water" (*abhiṣikta*) because he was invested with the royal throne. Regarding "the hidden treasure": this refers to the queen not having yet departed, as well as the gold, jewels, and so forth that were being controlled.
82. There was a non-Buddhist ascetic who, while traveling from the kingdom of Vatsa, stopped midway and left behind one thousand *pala*.
A multitude of bhikṣus walking behind him picked up a gold purse and said to one another, "Let us wait for those who come to search for it so that we may return it to them.
After the heretic had been gone for some time, they searched in every direction; finding the original purse, the bhikṣus immediately returned it.

The man, however, falsely claimed that the gold was insufficient, leading them to take the matter before the authorities. Upon investigation, the facts were established: the heretic’s claim was deficient, and the gold purse was confiscated by the government.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they resented that bhikṣu for his fussiness over discarded items and reported it to the Buddha; consequently, the Buddha established a rule.
Later, while practicing moderation in eating, the upāsikā Viśākhā thought to herself as she was going to visit the Buddha, "It is not necessary to be so elaborately adorned when visiting the Buddha.
Thus, she removed her ornaments and placed them under a tree before entering to see the Buddha. Upon leaving, she forgot to take them back.
A certain bhikṣu saw this and consequently established the rule not to take [any property]; he went and informed the World-Honored One, who therefore granted an exception, saying:
"Except for that which is within a saṃghārāma. Furthermore, another bhikṣu stayed overnight at a layperson's house where there was treasure;
the monk guarded it throughout the night without sleeping. He reported this to the Buddha, who likewise granted an exception for such cases.
83. [The case] originated with the monk Upananda, who entered a village at an improper time to play dice with a layperson.
A former acquaintance of that layperson became jealous and harbored resentment toward the monk for entering the village at an improper time. When the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule;
"playing dice" refers here to gambling with money.

84. When Kāḷudāyin anticipated that the Buddha would come along this path, he prepared a high and wide seat upon the road and said to the Buddha, "Look at my bed and seat. It was for this reason that the Buddha established the rule.
85. At that time, the group of six monks made bedding out of *tūla* cotton. When a layperson saw this, he looked upon it with disapproval;

*tūla* is translated here as "fine and soft," and the Vinaya states it refers to the flowers of the white poplar, the *pūtaka*, and so forth. The Buddha heard of this and therefore established the prohibition.
86. In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a craftsman of faith who made needle-cases from ivory and horn for the bhikṣus.

Because all the bhikṣus ordered him to make them, his family business was completely abandoned and his livelihood and clothing became deficient. A bhikṣu content with what he had informed the Buddha of this situation.
[The Buddha] then established a formal rule.
87. While the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, on one day he did not go to a meal invitation. King Śeṣadatta sent food for the World-Honored One.

As it was the World-Honored One’s regular practice not to accept invitations, he surveyed the monks’ quarters and saw that in a secluded spot, the bedding and mats of the community had been spread out in the open air;
they were defiled by impurities and soaked by heavy rain. For this reason, he established the rule permitting the use of the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat).
88. At that time, because the group of six monks made their *niṣīdana* mats excessively large and long when covering their bedding, this was further regulated.
At that time, in Jeta’s Grove, various bhikṣus suffered from boils and sores, and the pus and blood defiled their bodies. The Buddha...
It was permitted to make a wound-covering cloth (*vaṇa-paṭṭaka*). However, when monks wore coarse woolen cloths over their wounds, they suffered pain as the cloth moved against them.

Consequently, the Buddha ordered that fine, soft wound-covering cloths be made. The group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) then made these cloths excessively large and long. Other monks reported this matter to the Buddha, and he therefore established the rule.
89. At that time, when Viśākhā requested a rain-bath robe (*vassikasāṭikā*), the group of six monks made robes of excessive size;
therefore, [the rule] was established. 90.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda’s stature was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha’s; when the bhikṣus saw Nanda from afar...
When the Buddha arrived at Dhānañjāni, they mistook him for the Buddha and all rose to welcome him; upon reaching him, they realized it was Nanda.
The monks reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha then commanded that Nanda should always wear black robes to distinguish himself from the others.

At that time, the group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) made robes equal in size to those of the Tathāgata or even larger than them. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a precept as the ninety-first *pārājika* offense.
The *pāyattika* rules are concluded.

○ Fourth, the *pratideśanīya* dharmas. In Sanskrit, *pratideśanīya* is translated as "confession toward another," meaning that when one commits an offense of this category, one must confess it face-to-face before another person.
First: At that time, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a famine and grain was expensive; the people were starving, and those who died were beyond counting.
It was difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain almsfood. On the first day, the bhikṣuṇī Padmāvatī obtained some food and gave it to the bhikṣus;
what she obtained on the second day and the third day she likewise gave to the bhikṣus, all at once while they were on the road.
A certain elder came begging for alms with a large retinue of carriages. The nun Utpalavarṇā moved aside onto the path to avoid them;
however, due to being faint from hunger, she fell into a pit and her face was buried in deep mud. Seeing this, the elder hurriedly ordered her to be helped up and asked what ailment she had.
The nun replied, "I am afflicted by hunger. Because of this exchange, as described above, this rule was established.

After the precept [was established], a sick bhikṣu did not dare to accept food from a nun who was not a relative; for this reason, the Buddha further formulated the rule regarding those who are "not ill.
Second, at that time, various bhikṣus in Jeta’s Grove were receiving [offerings] together with the group of six bhikṣus (Ṣaḍvargika) in the homes of laypeople.
There were six groups of bhikṣuṇīs who, on behalf of the six groups of bhikṣus, requested soup and rice; at this place, they exchanged their respective duties and provided the food.
Because other bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, he established this regulation.
Third: At that time, there was a householder in the city of Rājagṛha whose husband and wife were both of right faith and delighted in giving.
They constantly provided alms to the bhikṣus who came begging, never failing for a single day. Because of this, they became impoverished.
Other householders remarked, "That family was formerly wealthy, yet because of their giving of food to the Saṃgha, they have been reduced to poverty. When the bhikṣus heard this...

They went and informed the World-Honored One. The Buddha, for this reason, permitted the Saṃgha to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) regarding householders who are "householders under training" (*śaikṣa-kuṭumbika*).
By performing this *karman*, monks were not to beg for alms from their homes. "Householders under training" refers to the families of those who study the Path but are poor;
therefore, this precept was established. Furthermore, there were monks who had previously accepted an invitation from such a household.
Because of this regulation, [the laypeople] did not dare to go again, and the sick bhikṣu also did not dare to accept food from a family under a vow of restraint;
thus he informed the Buddha, whereupon the Buddha established a further regulation, adding the words "previously invited" and "not being ill."
The fourth: While the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Garden at Kapilavastu, women from the city went to the monastery bearing food.
On the way, they were harassed by bandits. Because the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule:
"If a bhikṣu resides in an araṇya or a remote and dangerous place, he must not accept food outside the boundaries of the saṃghārāma."
When receiving food within a *saṃghārāma*, one should confess the transgression to another bhikṣu.

At that time, because a sick bhikṣu was afraid to accept and carry food due to this regulation, he informed the Buddha of the matter; consequently, the rule was further amended by including the phrase "unless one is ill.
Thus concludes the aforementioned four methods of confession.
○ One Hundred Rules of Training (Śaikṣa-dharmas) The Vinaya-piṭaka states: *śaikṣakaraṇīya-dharmāḥ*. This is translated as "rules that should be learned.
It is also called *duṣkṛta*, which is translated as "misdeed" (*èzuò*). This is the lightest category of offense.

The following one hundred items were all enacted due to the conduct of the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika-bhikṣu*); their textual characteristics are clear and need not be cited in detail. [Note: The group of six monks.]
As for the names: first, Icchantika; second, Kālodāyin; third, Saṃthadaṭṭa; fourth, Maheśadaṭṭa; fifth, Assaji; sixth, Puṇṇa.
According to the sixteenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the term "Purā" is a Sanskrit word whose meaning is not detailed in the Tibetan canon and is not translated there.
Elsewhere it is stated that "Vatsaputra" is its equivalent, which is translated as "Calf" (*vatsa*).
My son, this must surely be an abbreviation of a Sanskrit term; what is described above is likely the *vṛṣaṇaka* (the "scrotum" garment).

Although I have examined various sources extensively, none provide a detailed account. Thus, the *Mingyi ji* states: "The Sanskrit term for *pūlā* is correctly *puṭṭhala*; it is translated as 'short-cuffed boots.'"
○ The Seven Methods for Settling Disputes: Because these seven methods are able to settle all disputes of the past, present, and future, [the first is]:

"When the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) should be granted, one must grant the *saṃmukhavinaya*. Here, "presence" (*saṃmukha*) refers to the presence of the person, the presence of the *Dharma*, and the presence of the *Saṃgha*.

In the Vinaya, this is translated as "extinguishing evil. The first phrase refers to investigating and weighing the facts; the second phrase refers to administering a disciplinary measure to settle the dispute.

The subsequent cases follow this pattern. That is to say, when a senior monk (*sthavira*) who oversees affairs investigates a matter thoroughly, he should determine that it ought to be extinguished in the present.
If one performs a confession before four witnesses, then the matter of dispute will be extinguished.
Second, one should grant the *smṛti-vinaya* (discipline of recollection) when it is appropriate to grant the *smṛti-vinaya*. "Recollection" refers to past events;

for instance, there may be a bhikṣu who previously committed an offense but later, when the matter is raised, forgets it. One then causes him to recollect it so that he may confess before the assembly.
How could he have falsely accused someone of something that did not exist? Yet, sometimes [the accusation] is made despite its non-existence.
Since there are also cases where the root offense is manifest, if mindfulness and recollection are present, one should reform; if they are absent, one should exert effort.
Thus, contentious matters will cease.
Third, in cases where the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of non-delusion) should be granted, one must grant the *amūḷhavinaya*. "Non-delusion" refers to when...
A bhikṣu, being deranged and mentally disturbed, committed many offenses.
Later, when his madness had subsided, the other bhikṣus raised the matter of the offenses he had committed and asked him, "Do you remember them? He replied, "I do not remember them;
I committed these various offenses by mistake while I was deranged. This was not done intentionally. Even so, the bhikṣus continued to press him without ceasing, whereupon he addressed them.

The Buddhas have ordained that for one who commits an act of non-insanity (*amūḍha-vinaya*), the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) shall be performed within the assembly;
once the motion has been completed, the dispute is thereby extinguished, and this is termed "non-insanity.
Fourth, one who deserves the penalty of confession (*pratijñā-kāraka*) should be granted the penalty of confession. "Confession" refers to a bhikṣu who has committed an offense.

Regarding the characteristics of the confession of one's own offense: if a bhikṣu has committed an evil deed—whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, or the like—he may declare his offense based on that transgression through the procedure of "confession by one's own word" (*yathā-vādita-vinaya*).
This means that the bhikṣu who has committed the offense should go before a pure bhikṣu, baring one shoulder, prostrating at his feet with palms joined, and personally state the name of the offense.
If one confesses their own offenses before an elder and does not conceal them, and the Sangha accepts the confession, then the dispute is settled.
Fifth, when the offense is equivalent to a *tassapāpiyasika* (an offense requiring further search), it should be dealt with as a *tassapāpiyasika*. According to the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*.
5. One who should be dealt with according to the *pāpikā-ājñā* (finding fault) is to be dealt with according to the *pāpikā-ājñā*. 6.
One who should be dealt with according to the *tassapāpiyasika* (further finding fault) is to be dealt with according to the *tassapāpiyasika*. In the Fang edition, the sixth is made the fifth;

"many finding fault" (*bahujana-pāpikā-ājñā*) is the same as "many finding fault" (*tassapāpiyasika*). This refers to the meaning of examining the facts closely and with certainty. Or, there may be a bhikṣu...
When a matter lies within the realm of doubt, one must investigate it according to the facts;

thus, by meticulously examining the nature and gravity of the offense, the inner circle will find no grounds for complaint regarding the administration of justice, and the dispute will be extinguished.
Sixth, one should grant the *mānāpya* (probation) that corresponds to the offense for which it is sought;

this refers to the "confession before the assembly" as described in the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Regarding the "offense for which [the probation] is sought," the intent is to declare the offense before the community.
That is to say, if a bhikṣu’s actions are manifest and the truth is beyond doubt, one then administers punishment according to the facts to make it clear.
Because it is based on reality, there is no need to seek much; thus, by excluding the word "much," when there is balance in dealing with affairs, contentious matters will be extinguished.
Seventh, "one should grant [the *pārivāsika*] like grass covering the ground" means one should grant it like grass covering the ground. This is explained by way of a simile;
according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, fascicle 48, it refers to a bhikṣu who has committed many offenses that are contrary to the dharma of a śramaṇa and are evil.
Regarding those who speak without moderation, enter or exit improperly, and commit offenses, they reflect upon themselves, thinking: "I have committed many offenses;
fearing that my transgressions are grave and heavy, it would not be as well to follow the Buddha's teaching. Consequently, the assembly remains in a state of unease.

Thereupon, [the offender] approaches the elders and senior monks (*sthavira*), confesses their own offenses, and hopes that the elders will graciously grant them leave to perform a confession (*pratideśanā*)—a sincere repentance like grass covering the ground.
"Guilt is like grass covering the ground; by this principle, the matter of dispute is extinguished. Furthermore, grass covering the ground is a beautiful sign of compliance and submission.
Why is this? Because when one of superior virtue presides over the multitude, they are majestic without being stern.
Others revere their virtue and thus submit their hearts and follow them, just as grass covers what lies beneath. It is also as described in the *Lü Yǔ* (The Discourse of Lù):"

This means that the virtue of the superior man is like the wind, while the virtue of the common people is like the grass; the grass inevitably bends when it encounters the wind. The principle is much the same.
The Vinaya-piṭaka merely lists the seven matters without detailing their specific characteristics, as these are found scattered elsewhere.

Therefore, this [text] synthesizes their meaning and embellishes the phrasing; the determination of their significance is as stated above. If one wishes to examine them in detail, one may consult the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra.

Having assembled the community through the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, one should perform the act of *codanā* (reproach) against him; having performed the *codanā*, one should perform the act of *smṛti* (remembrance); and having performed the *smṛti*, one should then impose the offense.
The Meaning of the Origins of the *Caturvargika-prātimokṣa-sūtra* (End)
